params.textField: Currently in Australia, hypertension is defined as systolic (from the Greek word meaning "a drawing together, contraction") of *140* mmHg over diastolic (from the Greek word meaning “dilation”) of *90* mmHg or greater. Systolic pre-hypertension is defined as *120* to *139* and is associated with an 55% to 71% increased risk of cardiovascular disease and stroke as compared to individuals who have a blood pressure of 115/75 or less. There are two broad classifications of hypertension, being Primary (also called *essential*) hypertension and secondary hypertension. A person whose hypertension is caused by renal arterial occlusion is considered to have *secondary* hypertension, which should resolve after the single problem is addressed. Conversely, *primary* hypertension has several risk factors including some genetic causes, smoking, poor diets, sedentary lifestyle, obesity and others.

params.textField: Hypertension is one of the many disorders that results in a spiral of events that all end up perpetuating the initial problem and leading to the damage of many different organs. Initially the hypertension can damage the blood vessels, contributing to hardening of the arteries, known as *atherosclerosis*, which narrows the lumen of the artery, leading to even higher blood pressure. The blood vessel damage can also weaken the walls of the arteries, leading to *aneurysms* that can get larger because interestingly, the pressure inside will increase as the damaged vessel forms a bubble-like projection. The arteries in the *glomerulus* of the nephrons are particularly sensitive to the high blood pressure, which can lead to chronic renal failure, and the arteries in the *retina* of the eyes are also sensitive. The build up of plaques on the walls of the arteries can progress and become unstable, leading to heart attacks and strokes. In clinic, we do not generally say that the client “has atherosclerosis”. Instead, if atherosclerosis is contributing to for instance, a decrease in cognition, it is called *cerebral vascular disease*. If the atherosclerosis results in renal arterial occlusion, impotence, or loss of limbs, it is called *peripheral artery disease* and if the atherosclerosis is in the heart, it is called *coronary artery disease*.
